Seminar Title:

Design and Fabrication of PLA microneedles by 3D printing and micromachining

Abstract:

Polymeric microneedles (MNs) have emerged as a promising platform for transdermal drug delivery due to their minimal invasiveness, reduced pain, and ability to bypass first-pass metabolism; however, their widespread application is limited by inadequate mechanical strength, suboptimal tip sharpness, and challenges in scalable fabrication. In this study, we compared the mechanical performance of polylactic acid (PLA) microneedles fabricated using two approaches: (1) conventional fused deposition modeling (FDM) 3D printing, and (2) a hybrid method involving 3D-printed cylindrical posts followed by solventassisted mechanical turning. In the latter, the posts were immersed in acetone for 5 seconds to 5 minutes, air-dried, and then subjected to precision turning under constant force to refine the microneedle tip geometry. This solvent treatment facilitated controlled surface softening, improving machinability and enabling sharper tip formation. Finite Element Method (FEM) simulations in ANSYS were conducted to analyze stress distributions, predict skinpuncture behavior, and estimate the critical buckling load using experimentally measured geometries. The results demonstrated that post-processed microneedles exhibited enhanced mechanical stability and penetration capability compared to directly printed structures. Specifically, microneedles with a microneedle tip showed improved tip sharpness, a more favorable stress distribution, and greater resistance to deformation under axial loading. These findings indicate that solvent-assisted mechanical turning is an effective and scalable post-processing strategy to overcome the limitations of FDM-fabricated microneedles, thereby enhancing their structural integrity and functional performance for transdermal drug delivery applications. Keywords—Microneedle, 3D printing, FDM, FEM, Mechanical testing, skin insertion tests
